A Tale of Two Games: Great Foundation, Frustrating Execution Counter-Strike 2 is a difficult game to review. On one hand, it’s a necessary and often beautiful modernization of a timeless classic. On the other, it feels like a step back in several key areas that made its predecessor, CS:GO, the gold standard for competitive shooters for over a decade. After hundreds of hours in CS2, my feelings are as mixed as the community's, but the core of what makes Counter-Strike great is still here.  The Good:  Visual and Audio Overhaul: The game looks and sounds fantastic. The lighting on the updated maps is a massive improvement, making familiar locations feel fresh and new. Gun sounds are punchier, and the overall audio design is more immersive.  Game-Changing Smokes: The new volumetric smoke is a genuine innovation. The ability to clear smoke with grenades or have it react to gunfire adds a whole new tactical layer to the game. It's one of the best new features and fundamentally changes how chokepoints are contested.  Premier Mode: The concept of a global and regional ranking system is a great addition. It gives players a clear path for progression and a reason to take competitive play seriously outside of third-party platforms.  The Bad:  The "CS:GO Feel" is Gone: This is the most common complaint, and it's a valid one. The movement and shooting mechanics feel different. There's a noticeable "peeker's advantage" where the player swinging a corner often has a significant edge. This can make holding angles feel like a disadvantage, which is a major departure from traditional Counter-Strike.  Rampant Cheating: The cheating problem is as bad as it's ever been. It's especially prevalent in Premier mode, which undermines the entire ranking system. Without a more robust anti-cheat, it's hard to stay motivated to climb the ladder.  Missing Content: At launch, CS2 was missing many of the maps, game modes, and community features that made CS:GO so beloved. While some of this has been added back, the game still feels somewhat barebones in comparison.  The Verdict:  So, should you play Counter-Strike 2? If you're a die-hard fan of the series, you're probably already playing it and have your own list of pros and cons. If you're a new player, CS2 is a great-looking and accessible entry point into the world of tactical shooters, but be prepared for a steep learning curve and some frustrating moments.  For the returning CS:GO veterans, my recommendation is a cautious "Yes." The core of Counter-Strike is still here, and it's still one of the most rewarding competitive experiences in gaming. However, you'll need to adapt to the new feel of the game and have the patience to deal with its current shortcomings. CS2 has the potential to be a worthy successor to CS:GO, but it's not quite there yet. It's a game built on a fantastic foundation that is currently held back by a number of frustrating issues.

Death is a great teacher. Failure in Counter-Strike: Global Offensive is, as it always has been for this series, the greatest way to learn where you should have gone, what you shouldn't have done, and how you could have done better. Counter-Strike players spend a lot of time learning -- consequently, they are always getting better.    Growth is an important factor in Global Offensive, especially if you're coming into Counter-Strike fresh or after a sabbatical. This is an extremely hardcore, skill-based first-person shooter, and it forces you to think differently than other modern shooters. If you’re a Call of Duty player, you’re going to need to change your play style to succeed here. Counter-Strike also tries developing into something new here as well, despite doing little to push itself beyond what it’s always done best. Global Offensive modifies old maps to keep veterans on their toes, and introduces official new modes that encourage different play styles for the first time in almost 15 years.    For the uninitiated, Counter-Strike: Global Offensive is a small-scale, team-based first-person shooter with permanent death. When a counter-terrorist kills a terrorist planting explosives in a classic Defusal match, or a CT escort swallows a sniper round in Hostage Rescue, the victim is dead for good and doesn't respawn until the next round. As such, players on both sides must exercise skill and care. The bomb objective, meanwhile, gives everyone a purpose. Of course matches end when everyone on a team is dead, but a clever and coordinated terrorist team will give the CTs the slip, plant their bomb, and protect the bomb site. Between rounds, everyone spends earned cash on better gear and guns, and the cycle continues.    Pieces of the Counter-Strike formula are dated at this point, but the superb heart and soul of Global Offensive is timeless. Teams are small, guns are lethal, and rounds are short. There's an addictive just-one-more-round quality to it, because there's a constant desire to do better than last time, to earn a satisfying kill, or to win in a new way. Call of Duty and Battlefield vets will wonder why they can't sprint to escape enemy fire or look down the iron sights to improve aim; Counter-Strike players will feel like they walked into their redecorated home. Certain map redesigns will catch hardcore fans off guard, but the changes are for the best -- the underpass choke point in de_dust, for instance, has a new escape route.    Even in the face of genre evolution, Global Offensive doesn’t care to adapt. CSGO is so dedicated to Counter-Strike's aging ideals despite market and trend changes that it brute-forces its way to success. Part of what makes it such an engaging competitive game is that killing in Global Offensive requires a wholly different skill set than other shooters. Everyone is limited to what they have and can see, with little room for character modification or on-the-fly advantages. Running and gunning is a useless play style, even if you've bought a helmet and kevlar that round, to the point that someone standing still is more likely to score the kill. Walking, crouching, or standing are your best bets to reduce the inaccurate spray of machine-gun fire.    Consequently, killing in Global Offensive feels good. There's a sickening sensation to dropping someone dead because you know they're not coming back. It's also satisfying knowing you used limited resources to play smarter than your victim. If players aren't watching corners, providing covering fire, or using smoke grenades and flashbangs, they're more likely to take a headshot from a more delicate and patient triggerman. The desire to experience that distinct feeling is a strong motivator to keep playing, even when you're getting steamrolled by an obviously better team.    If you've played Counter-Strike before, Global Offensive probably sounds a whole lot like Counter-Strike. Like Counter-Strike: Source before it, Global Offensive exists simply to modernize the look of the classic competitive shooter, while doing little to disrupt the core form and function. At the same time, it does enough to color outside the lines of tradition to justify your time and effort.    Fire is one of the most interesting new combat variables. Molotov cocktails and incendiary grenades either roast groups of guys or force them in another direction. Flames are a useful distraction or scare tactic, too. They're particularly useful during Demolition matches, which focus the fight at a single bomb site rather than giving terrorists two to pick between. The new and modified maps in this mode aren't as big as classic Counter-Strike arenas – entire sections have been cut off to direct teams toward a central location – but their thoughtful design is as intricate as ever. The Lake map is a standout -- there's a wide open yet densely populated yard around the bomb site, which is inside a sizable lakeside home with plenty of vantage points and hiding spots. To separate Demolition from Defusal, players can't buy between rounds. Instead, it takes a cue from the other new mode, Arms Race, in which each kill unlocks another weapon instantly. The better you do, the more you have to switch up the way you play, and because Demolition is so fast you'll need to be quick on your feet.    Unlike other game types, Arms Race allows for respawns. It's the most chaotic and care-free mode in Global Offensive, with players throwing caution to the wind for the sake of climbing the kill ladder as quickly as possible. It's a shame there are only two maps in Arms Race -- a problem that will more likely persist on consoles than PC.    If you have the option, playing the PC version is unquestionably the best way to experience Counter-Strike: Global Offensive. Mods, mouse and keyboard, and the usual PC-only options are better than the ports. Plus, Valve is much better about long-term PC support -- it abandoned Team Fortress 2 on consoles, and Portal 2's level editor was PC exclusive. If you prefer to play on consoles, Global Offensive is the same great game

I’ve been diving into Counter-Strike 2 and honestly, the shooting mechanics are phenomenal. Every shot feels tight, recoil control actually matters, and when you hit that clean headshot, it’s just chef’s kiss. Valve really nailed the gunplay—it’s smooth, satisfying, and it feels like the most polished version of Counter-Strike we’ve ever had.    Movement though? It’s just… ok. It gets the job done, but compared to CSGO, it feels clunky and off. CS:GO’s movement was sharp and precise—every strafe, jump, and peek had this satisfying rhythm. CS2 just doesn’t capture that same flow, and it honestly feels like a downgrade by a mile.    And then there’s the big one: the anti-cheat. Still garbage. This has been an issue since CSGO, and somehow CS2 is still plagued with it. Running into wallhackers and spin-bots after all these years is beyond frustrating. Like, what’s the point of mastering recoil and movement if some cheater just ace wallbang headshot you 6 layers into the brick wall in five minutes? It honestly kills the vibe of what could be a near-perfect game.    So yeah, CS2 has the best shooting mechanics in the business, but weaker movement and the same old anti-cheat problem drag it down hard. Valve, please fix this already.

Esto es muy importante para que luego los ñoquis de papa no se desarmen, ya que al cocerlas con cáscara evitamos que absorban agua en exceso. Hacemos un corte horizontal por todo el contorno de la papa, en el video se ve bien, y las llevamos a una olla con agua. Cocinar hasta que al pincharlas se caigan. Pisamos las papas todavía en caliente como todo puré digno, agregamos sal, pimienta y mezclamos super bien. Agregamos el huevo batido y la harina. No le vamos a agregar toda la harina de una, nos vamos a guardar un poco para ver cómo viene. Las cantidades son más bien proporcionales, puede ser que la papa haya absorbido más agua o que el huevo sea más chico, así que vamos a agregar la harina de a poco.    Unir con la mano hasta que se pueda pasar hasta la mesada y terminar de integrar. Si en este paso ven que hace falta más harina, tenemos el resto para agregar. Ahora viene la magia, vamos a pasarlos por la herramienta para darle forma a los ñoquis de papa de arriba hacia abajo. Counter-Strike 2 is about order and chaos. Terrorists plant bombs, counter-terrorists defuse them. Lives are lost in seconds. But for me, the real battlefield isn’t the map. It’s the inventory screen.  Opening cases is… different. I’ve spent years studying blood patterns, dissecting corpses, understanding human behavior. None of that prepared me for watching a gold slide past my screen, only to land on a blue worth nothing less than pocket lint. It’s the same feeling as finding a blood trail that leads nowhere... frustration  Pros: -Shooting feels precise, like a scalpel. -Defusing bombs scratches the same itch as cleaning up a crime scene. -Occasionally, a teammate actually listens to strategy. Rare, but satisfying.  When you do open something rare from a case, it’s like leaving a scene perfectly spotless... pure relief  Cons: -Most teammates have the tactical awareness of my victims—blind and predictable. -Cases cost more than body bags, and deliver less.  Final thoughts: Counter-Strike 2 is a lesson in control—sometimes you have it, sometimes you don’t. But whether it’s cleaning up after a mess or finally unboxing that knife, the result is the same satisfaction.  ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (5/5)

As a kid, I dreamed of becoming an astronaut, but instead I decided to try Counter-Strike 2… and I still went to space – just because of the Desert Eagle’s recoil.    CS2 made me realize my reactions are slower than my grandma’s internet connection when she’s watching YouTube on mobile data. I join a match hoping to get at least one kill, but I end up with 0/17 and the MVP award for “most beautiful fall after a headshot.”    The graphics are amazing – you can see every detail, even your tears hitting the keyboard after someone with the nickname “xXx\_P3pSiM4n\_xXx” stabs you in the back. The new Source 2 engine is so realistic that when I throw a flashbang, I get blinded in real life… and my upstairs neighbor is now asking why I’m screaming “BLIND!!!” in the middle of the night.    The gun mechanics are unique – mine always shoots sideways, while my opponent’s gun has a built-in GPS that guides every bullet straight into my forehead. The smoke is “dynamic,” which means I can’t see anything… except for the enemy, who can apparently see perfectly through it because he’s graduated from Hogwarts and mastered the spell “Wallhackus Maximus.”    CS2 has taught me some valuable life lessons:    * Never run with a knife… unless you want to die faster.  * Never trust a “teammate” who says “EZ WIN” at the start of the round.  * And most importantly: life is short, but the defuse-without-a-kit animation is eternal.    I love this game because every match is different – sometimes I die in 3 seconds, sometimes in 5. Sometimes we win, but that happens so rarely it feels like spotting a unicorn.    I recommend CS2 to anyone who wants to test their patience, nervous system, and how hard they can slam a desk before it breaks.

At first glance, Kyoko Hori is a popular, sociable, and impeccably put-together girl, admired by classmates for her beauty and charm. However, outside of school, she is completely different — a simple, down-to-earth young woman who spends her days caring for her younger brother and managing household chores, far from the image of a glamorous high school idol.  Izumi Miyamura, on the other hand, appears at school to be a quiet, withdrawn, and slightly awkward boy with thick glasses — the kind of student people dismiss as a nerd. But beyond the school gates, he reveals a completely different side: long hair, tattoos, piercings, and a gentle, compassionate personality hidden beneath his reserved exterior.  A chance encounter between Hori and Miyamura outside of school becomes the spark for an unexpected friendship, which gradually blossoms into a romantic relationship. Together, they begin to share their deepest secrets, fears, and vulnerabilities, learning to accept themselves without the masks they wear in public, and finding in each other the comfort and understanding they’ve been missing.  Beyond the main couple, the story also shines a light on their friends, creating a warm, lively portrayal of school life — where humor intertwines with touching moments, and small everyday events take on special meaning.  Horimiya is not just a romance — it’s a story about self-acceptance, the value of honesty, and the importance of having someone who sees you for who you truly are. CS2 Review – Great Game, But the Cheaters & Trust Factor Suck  CS2 is honestly a blast to play. The gunplay feels super clean, movement is smooth, and the mechanics are the best in pvp shooter games. new subtick system is meh and 64 tick would be better with shots registering however it works decent enough so cant complain much . obviously graphics revamp being good  Gameplay-wise, it’s top-tier. Whether you’re clutching a 1v4 or lining up perfect utility, the game really rewards skill and timing. It feels good to play — when it works properly.  But here’s the catch: cheaters are everywhere, and it kills the experience fast. Even in Prime, you'll still run into spinbots, wallers, or people that just feel off. VAC Live doesn’t seem to be catching much in real-time, and it’s honestly frustrating when you’re trying to play legit.  And then there's the Trust Factor system, which seems completely messed up. If you’re on a newer account or haven’t dumped thousands of hours into Steam, good luck. You'll get thrown into lobbies with blatant cheaters or super toxic teammates while older accounts with shady pasts get better games. It feels super biased and makes playing on a fresh or clean account feel like a punishment.  Overall, CS2 is a great game at its core, but the matchmaking experience needs serious fixing. If Valve ever sorts out the cheaters and reworks Trust Factor to be fairer, this game would be unstoppable.  8/10 – Amazing gameplay, but ruined too often by cheaters and bad matchmaking.

The tension, the strategy, the adrenaline rush of a 1v3 clutch — CS2 delivers all of it, but with a polish that finally reflects the greatness the series has always deserved.  What moved me the most, though, was how familiar it still felt. Stepping onto Dust II again felt like walking into a childhood home that had been beautifully renovated. CS2 isn’t a reboot. It’s a love letter. To the veterans who remember 1.6. To the Global Elite grinders. To the first-time players discovering the thrill of their first ace. This game saved my life.  I am 30.  My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and adopted our son together. They are now both 4 years old.  When we were going through our separation, I found myself lost and miserable. I was self destructive. I got so mad one day from everything spiraling out of my control that I punched some concrete in a moment of overwhelming emotion. That caused me to break my 5th metacarpal in my right hand... my working hand... my games hand.. the hand that I held and carried my children to bed with.. The hand I desperately needed to make sure I could continue to provide.  After learning of the severity of my self-inflicted damage, I was borderline suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man with no history of depression or anxiety. I have never had fits of rage, or been one to break down and cry, but I was in a low spot that just really buried me from being able to see the light on the other side.  Having nothing better to do, I searched for a game I could play, ONE HANDED while I recovered. I somehow stumbled upon this game and read some of the reviews. I decided that it had to be worth a shot... I must admit, I didn't beat the game, or play nearly as long as some of you. In fact, I may have only played this game a day or two.. With that being said, after doing so, I had a new found joy and hope for life. I was able to put behind me the pain and suffering that had been cast over me. I was able to experience other peoples joy and happiness. I was able to see the fruits of my "labor". I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ minutes to this music long enough to realize that I was going to be okay.  After coming to that realization, I turned the game off, and I went back to work. It hurt my hand like hell but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so damn sorry for myself, and I became the father I needed to be in that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving as.  Today, I am close friend with my kids mother. We don't fight, or argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents, and friends.  I now have 3 kids. My third child is, wait for it, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my own separation, and we just stumbled in to each others life unexpectedly. We have been in a relationship for a year now, and are very happy together.  Moral of the story, you never know what life holds in store for you, and if I would have given up when all the odds were stacked against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Counter-Strike 2 had so much potential, but Valve dropped the ball hard.  Sure, the Source 2 engine brings better lighting and fancy smoke physics — but good luck enjoying any of that when the core gameplay is worse than CS:GO. The hit reg is all over the place, movement feels floaty, and the sub-tick system is either broken or just plain bad. It doesn’t feel like a tactical shooter anymore — it feels like a tech demo with spray patterns.  And don’t get me started on cheaters. The game is absolutely infested. Wallhacks, aimbots, spinbots — take your pick. The anti-cheat clearly isn’t doing its job, and reports feel meaningless. Ranked is basically unplayable unless you want to guess who’s legit and who’s scripting.  On top of that, the UI is clunky, servers feel inconsistent, and community features like mods and workshop maps are half-supported or missing entirely. And somehow they thought it was a good idea to replace CS:GO with this instead of running both side by side?  If you're looking for competitive integrity, polished mechanics, and a fair experience — CS2 is not it. This feels more like an early beta than a full release.

I've been a long-time Counter-Strike player and was genuinely disappointed with how CS2 replaced CS:GO. While I appreciate the addition of dynamic smokes, most of the gameplay changes have negatively impacted the experience for me.    Performance has noticeably declined — where I used to get 400+ FPS on certain maps in CS:GO, I now struggle to get stable frames in CS2. Hit registration feels inconsistent, movement is clunky, and the peeker's advantage is too strong, making it hard to hold angles reliably.    The removal of Overwatch and reliance on VAC Live has not helped with the cheating problem. There's a real need for a better anti-cheat system, as matches often feel compromised.    I'm also frustrated by the decision to remove CS:GO entirely, unlike how Source and 1.6 were kept separate in the past. Many of us would have preferred CS2 to be its own game instead of a forced upgrade.    The map rotation choices are also questionable. Personally, I loved Anubis and was disappointed to see it removed instead of a less popular map like Dust2.    Finally, I hope Valve starts putting more resources into improving core gameplay and listening to player feedback, rather than focusing so heavily on monetization through skins and cases.    I keep playing because I’ve invested so much time into this series, but I honestly don’t enjoy it like I used to. I miss CS:GO.

Counter-Strike 2 Review: Volumetric Smokes and the Need to Move On    Counter-Strike 2 is a slick, high-friction reinvention of a game that never really needed fixing. And yet, somehow, it works. Movement feels tight, gunplay is brutally efficient, and the new Source 2 engine adds a strange, almost hypnotic energy to the maps—like they’re alive, humming under your feet, quietly urging you to make a move to someplace a little more right for you.    That’s always been the spirit of CS: finding the right place, at the right time, with the right angle. A town, maybe. A town to keep you groovin’. One that rewards quick decisions, sharp reflexes, and a willingness to talk about it—over and over again. Mid push? Talk about it. Utility timing? Talk about it. Solo queueing? You're gonna talk about it all night in Discord.    And when the round begins, you don’t just run—you move on. There’s something rhythmic about it. You’ve got to move. You’ve got to move. The tempo in your head isn’t just adrenaline; it’s that quiet compulsion to rotate fast, to peak the corner just so, to listen for audio cues like you’re tuning a groove.    And whether you’re carrying bombsite A or just holding garage with a Nova and a dream, there's that persistent voice, subtle but steady: Won’t you take me there? Maybe not in words—but in vibe. You know it. You've felt it. A place where your shots land and your pings stabilize. A better ping. A better round. A better town. The right town.    The maps? Sharper, glossier. Mirage feels like it got a deep tissue massage. Dust2 still smells like home—burnt rubber, broken dreams, and flashbangs. Inferno? It’s a place with energy, with momentum. A place you want to stay in, but also... move through. Something about it just makes you want to keep grooving.    It’s not perfect. You’ll get tilted. You’ll get eco’d. You’ll get absolutely deleted by someone whose entire personality is bound to their butterfly knife skin. But you’ll load back in. Every time. Hoping—begging, really—that maybe this round, your team will finally take you there.    Somewhere new.  Somewhere smoother.  Somewhere funkier.    8.5/10  Valve didn’t just remaster CS—they whispered to the soul of every solo-queued player: Won’t you take me to a better game?  And then they did.  Welcome to CS2.

Prep the vegetables: Slice the eggplant, zucchini, squash, and tomato into thin, even rounds (~1/8 inch thick). Try to keep sizes similar for even cooking.  3. The July 29 CS2 update introduced more problems than improvements, and most of the changes feel rushed, untested, and disconnected from what players actually want.    Movement/Bhop is broken  Previously, you could jump from any surface by timing your second jump (bhop mechanic). Now, that second jump doesn't always register, even with perfect timing. It feels like there's artificial input delay or a cooldown on air movement. This ruins the flow and skill expression of movement. Bring back consistent bhop behavior — it was part of CS's identity.    Skin bugs (black textures and visual glitches)  Many skins — especially Field-Tested or Battle-Scarred — now appear covered in black patches or broken textures. It literally looks like someone pasted the wrong material onto the skin. This destroys the appeal of skins and affects items people paid real money for.    Weapon animations are buggy and overdone  AnimGraph2 is a cool idea, but it was poorly implemented. When inspecting the AK-47, the character's hand clips through the weapon. It looks broken. Animations feel overcomplicated and janky instead of smooth and satisfying.    The shooting mechanics were changed again — why?  CS2 shooting was already controversial, but people adjusted. Now it's changed again — the recoil timing feels different, bullets feel delayed, and spraying feels wrong. Why keep changing core shooting mechanics after players already adapted?    AK-47 draw sound is awful  The new draw sound for the AK-47 is flat-out unpleasant. It doesn’t sound powerful or clean — just off. This is a small thing, but sound in CS has always been critical, and this one feels like a downgrade.    Please stop reinventing core mechanics and visuals every patch. Fix what’s broken, but don’t constantly alter fundamentals that define Counter-Strike.

Dear Valve,    Thank you. Truly. It takes a special kind of genius to simultaneously create one of the most legendary FPS franchises of all time and manage to fumble it at nearly every opportunity.    You gave us Counter-Strike — a game built on precision, skill, and tension. Then you gave us Counter-Strike 2 — a game built on... shattered promises, tick-rate cope, and smoke grenades with more processing power than Half-Life: Alyx.    Let’s break it down:    Communication: Or more accurately, the complete lack of it. Other devs do roadmaps, dev blogs, Twitter updates. You? You drop a patch with one sentence and vanish like you're working from Black Mesa after a resonance cascade. Are the devs okay? Blink twice in morse code if you need help.    Anticheat: VAC is so ineffective it might as well stand for "Virtually Assuring Cheaters." Do you just throw darts at a wall to decide bans? Because right now, it feels like you’ve outsourced anticheat to a Magic 8-Ball.    Matchmaking: The Premier system is like a luxury car with no wheels. Nice dashboard, clean look — but where are we going? Smurfs, cheaters, one-sided matchmaking, no party restrictions… It's almost impressive how bad it feels. Audio broken, performance tanked, features missing… and then silence. Bravo.    You treat one of the greatest communities in gaming like we’re an inconvenience. You don’t engage, you don’t explain, and when you finally do something, it’s like you deliberately miss the point.    So again, thank you — for reminding us that no matter how good a game is, indifference from its creators will always catch up eventually.    Sincerely,  A frustrated player who keeps playing because you made something amazing — and then forgot how to care for it.

Counter-Strike 2: The Tactical Masterpiece That Ruined My Life (And I Keep Saying 'One More')  I like Counter-Strike 2. I just don’t know why. Maybe it’s the tactical gameplay that sometimes rewards strategy — usually right before my teammate rushes mid with the bomb, a dream, and no armor. Again.  The gunplay is crisp 🎯, the maps are gorgeous, and when things click, it's pure magic. But between those moments? Welcome to Hell— where your enemies are suspiciously good, your teammates are suspiciously terrible, and the AI-supported anti-cheat is just a shy spectator in the corner, maybe taking notes but basically doing absolutely nothing.  Speaking of doing nothing: the report feature! It's that cute little placebo button you press after getting one-tapped through smoke by someone with a private profile and a 400-hour account. You report, smile, and imagine justice… but then remember Overwatch was removed, and nobody's actually watching. Probably not even the AI 🤖.  The community is a warm bath of toxicity ☣️, best enjoyed with earplugs and low expectations. Every match is a sociology experiment with at least one human megaphone screaming about ranks, politics, or their mother’s Wi-Fi.  And utility? A handful of players use grenades to control the map like grandmasters. The rest treat them like toys — blinding teammates, bouncing Molotovs off walls, or accidentally donating smokes to the enemy team like it’s charity 🎁.  Oh, and skins. My beautiful, pixelated financial mistake 💸. What started as one innocent case has now spiraled into a full-blown gambling addiction. I could’ve gone on vacation — instead, I own four StatTrak P250s and depression.  If you expect updates about stuff the players actually want — prepare to be amazed by yet another $3 case so Valve can milk you even more 🐄.  Still… I play. Every day. I load up, pray for a fair match, and get rewarded with emotional damage and an occasional clutch round that makes me forget everything I just said.  Final Verdict: 10/10 would suffer again.

The Good  Gunplay is still sharp.  Even with the tweaks to movement and feel, CS2 continues to deliver intense, rewarding rounds. Out-thinking and out-shooting your opponent is as satisfying as ever. The gun mechanics are still tight, and clutch moments are as exhilarating now as they were a decade ago.    The Source 2 upgrade brings visual improvements.  Volumetric smokes and updated lighting give the game a more modern look. The way utility interacts with the environment (especially how bullets and grenades now affect smoke) changes tactics in creative ways.    Matchmaking and Premier mode push the scene forward.  A global ranking system, tied to map-specific performance, is a step in the right direction. The game is clearly aimed at building a deeper competitive identity, even if it's still being refined.    Still the best when it works.  When all cylinders fire—your teammates communicate, hit reg behaves, and you’re in the zone—there’s nothing like it.    The Not-So-Good  Movement feels off.  Even after patches, something about how the player moves, jumps, and peeks feels floaty or disconnected. The CS:GO muscle memory fights against the physics in CS2. Small timings feel slightly delayed, like you’re underwater compared to the crisp precision of CS:GO.    Hit registration is inconsistent.  Sub-tick servers were promised to fix everything. Reality hasn't caught up to the marketing. Sometimes you land a perfect shot and it does nothing. Other times, you're dead before you even react. It doesn't ruin every match, but it's enough to notice—and it shouldn't be.    Missing modes and maps.  Half of the fun, casual modes from CS:GO are gone. Arms Race, Flying Scoutsman, and even classic maps like Cache and Train have vanished. If you liked anything beyond standard 5v5 competitive, your options feel severely limited.    And the Ugly: Skins  This is where it hurts. I’m someone who didn’t just play CS:GO—I lived in it. I collected skins over years. Traded, sold, bought. Not for profit, but because I loved the aesthetic, the individuality. My inventory was a digital scrapbook of my Counter-Strike experience.    When CS2 launched, the lighting overhaul and material changes completely altered how many skins look. The colors on Fades are dulled. Dopplers lost their deep, rich tones. Knives that once gleamed now look plastic or flat. The lighting engine completely changed the look of my inventory—and not for the better.    And there’s no fix. No “legacy mode.” No option to toggle the old look. Just a shrug and a patch note, and your once-rare, gorgeous skin now looks like a poorly rendered knockoff.    This isn't about money. It's about respect for time, taste, and history. I never needed skins to increase in value—but I did expect them to stay beautiful. I didn't spend hundreds of dollars to see my prized collection downgraded by a rendering engine.    Final Thoughts  CS2 is still the best tactical shooter out there. It’s the successor to a legacy title, and with time, it may surpass CS:GO in polish and popularity. The core gameplay remains addictive, challenging, and rewarding.    But if you were emotionally or financially invested in skins, just know you’re going to feel the sting. I still play, and I still love the game—but I can’t pretend the transition didn’t burn.    Recommended—but with eyes wide open.

Death is a great teacher. Failure in Counter-Strike: Global Offensive is, as it always has been for this series, the greatest way to learn where you should have gone, what you shouldn't have done, and how you could have done better. Counter-Strike players spend a lot of time learning -- consequently, they are always getting better.  Growth is an important factor in Global Offensive, especially if you're coming into Counter-Strike fresh or after a sabbatical. This is an extremely hardcore, skill-based first-person shooter, and it forces you to think differently than other modern shooters. If you’re a Call of Duty player, you’re going to need to change your play style to succeed here. Counter-Strike also tries developing into something new here as well, despite doing little to push itself beyond what it’s always done best. Global Offensive modifies old maps to keep veterans on their toes, and introduces official new modes that encourage different play styles for the first time in almost 15 years.  For the uninitiated, Counter-Strike: Global Offensive is a small-scale, team-based first-person shooter with permanent death. When a counter-terrorist kills a terrorist planting explosives in a classic Defusal match, or a CT escort swallows a sniper round in Hostage Rescue, the victim is dead for good and doesn't respawn until the next round. As such, players on both sides must exercise skill and care. The bomb objective, meanwhile, gives everyone a purpose. Of course matches end when everyone on a team is dead, but a clever and coordinated terrorist team will give the CTs the slip, plant their bomb, and protect the bomb site. Between rounds, everyone spends earned cash on better gear and guns, and the cycle continues.  Pieces of the Counter-Strike formula are dated at this point, but the superb heart and soul of Global Offensive is timeless. Teams are small, guns are lethal, and rounds are short. There's an addictive just-one-more-round quality to it, because there's a constant desire to do better than last time, to earn a satisfying kill, or to win in a new way. Call of Duty and Battlefield vets will wonder why they can't sprint to escape enemy fire or look down the iron sights to improve aim; Counter-Strike players will feel like they walked into their redecorated home. Certain map redesigns will catch hardcore fans off guard, but the changes are for the best -- the underpass choke point in de_dust, for instance, has a new escape route.  Even in the face of genre evolution, Global Offensive doesn’t care to adapt. CSGO is so dedicated to Counter-Strike's aging ideals despite market and trend changes that it brute-forces its way to success. Part of what makes it such an engaging competitive game is that killing in Global Offensive requires a wholly different skill set than other shooters. Everyone is limited to what they have and can see, with little room for character modification or on-the-fly advantages. Running and gunning is a useless play style, even if you've bought a helmet and kevlar that round, to the point that someone standing still is more likely to score the kill. Walking, crouching, or standing are your best bets to reduce the inaccurate spray of machine-gun fire.  Consequently, killing in Global Offensive feels good. There's a sickening sensation to dropping someone dead because you know they're not coming back. It's also satisfying knowing you used limited resources to play smarter than your victim. If players aren't watching corners, providing covering fire, or using smoke grenades and flashbangs, they're more likely to take a headshot from a more delicate and patient triggerman. The desire to experience that distinct feeling is a strong motivator to keep playing, even when you're getting steamrolled by an obviously better team.  If you've played Counter-Strike before, Global Offensive probably sounds a whole lot like Counter-Strike. Like Counter-Strike: Source before it, Global Offensive exists simply to modernize the look of the classic competitive shooter, while doing little to disrupt the core form and function. At the same time, it does enough to color outside the lines of tradition to justify your time and effort.  Fire is one of the most interesting new combat variables. Molotov cocktails and incendiary grenades either roast groups of guys or force them in another direction. Flames are a useful distraction or scare tactic, too. They're particularly useful during Demolition matches, which focus the fight at a single bomb site rather than giving terrorists two to pick between. The new and modified maps in this mode aren't as big as classic Counter-Strike arenas – entire sections have been cut off to direct teams toward a central location – but their thoughtful design is as intricate as ever. The Lake map is a standout -- there's a wide open yet densely populated yard around the bomb site, which is inside a sizable lakeside home with plenty of vantage points and hiding spots. To separate Demolition from Defusal, players can't buy between rounds. Instead, it takes a cue from the other new mode, Arms Race, in which each kill unlocks another weapon instantly. The better you do, the more you have to switch up the way you play, and because Demolition is so fast you'll need to be quick on your feet.  Unlike other game types, Arms Race allows for respawns. It's the most chaotic and care-free mode in Global Offensive, with players throwing caution to the wind for the sake of climbing the kill ladder as quickly as possible. It's a shame there are only two maps in Arms Race -- a problem that will more likely persist on consoles than PC.  If you have the option, playing the PC version is unquestionably the best way to experience Counter-Strike: Global Offensive. Mods, mouse and keyboard, and the usual PC-only options are better than the ports. Plus, Valve is much better about long-term PC support -- it abandoned Team Fortress 2 on consoles, and Portal 2's level editor was PC exclusive. If you prefer to play on consoles, Global Offensive is the same great game

Sometimes it feels like I was teleported back well further than the round trip time to the server. That feels terrible when it happens and honestly ruins the whole experience. It was a cool experiment, but "what you see is what you get" obviously didn't work out.

Welcome to Counter-Strike 2 — where aiming is optional, cheating is encouraged, and actual gameplay is just background noise.  Let’s face it: trying to play legit in CS2 feels like showing up to a gunfight with a spoon. Wallhacks, aimbots, spinbots — they’re not just common, they’re part of the ecosystem now. With no Overwatch, and an anti-cheat system that’s basically on vacation, you’d honestly be better off just downloading cheats yourself. It’s faster, easier, and apparently less risky than trying to improve.  Ranked mode? A masterpiece of chaos. You’ll either get matched with complete beginners who farmed 3,000 hours by leaving the game open, or against people who have "silver aim, global ego." Don’t worry though — rank doesn’t matter, because the system clearly doesn’t understand it either.  In casual respawn modes, things get even better! Most of your teammates will be AFK bots farming hours, boosting Steam stats for resale accounts. Gameplay? Interaction? Communication? Nah, just empty servers filled with scripts and idle timers. Peak experience.  And the cherry on top: the modern CS2 player. No longer defined by skill or gamesense — now it’s all about who spent $1,200 on a knife or flexes FaceIT level 10 while dodging in-game matchmaking like the plague. Why try in ranked when your inventory does the talking?  Even the reviews speak volumes. CS:GO? Overwhelmingly Positive. CS2? "Mixed" and dropping faster than your ELO after a cheater drops 40 kills on you.  At this point, cheating isn’t just tolerated — it’s meta. It’s genuinely more efficient to run scripts than to grind, communicate, or — god forbid — improve. Welcome to the future of Counter-Strike.  Play at your own risk. Or don’t. Honestly, you’re better off watching paint dry — fewer cheaters there.

My CS2 Review:  Counter-Strike 2 feels like both an upgrade and a letdown. The new graphics and sounds are great, and the volumetric smokes are a cool addition that actually impact gameplay. Weapons like the AK and AWP feel smooth and satisfying. But despite the improvements, CS2 still feels unfinished.  The subtick servers were hyped, but hit registration can still feel inconsistent. Movement feels heavier compared to CS:GO, and classic mechanics like strafing and bhopping aren't as fluid. The new Premier mode is interesting and gives a ranked grind, but the matchmaking experience can be frustrating.  CS2 has potential to surpass CS:GO, but right now it’s held back by bugs, performance issues, and a feeling that Valve rushed it out too early.  Pros:  Great graphics and updated sound design.  Volumetric smokes change the game.  Weapons feel powerful and rewarding.  Premier mode adds competitive structure.   Cons:  Movement feels clunky.  Hit registration is inconsistent.  Matchmaking can feel unbalanced.   Overall: CS2 is a good foundation for the future, but as of now, it still feels like early access. I hope Valve keeps updating and improving it.

[h1]CS2’s steep learning curve rewards skill like no other shooter.[/h1]  [i]For over two decades, Counter-Strike has offered an elite competitive experience, one shaped by millions of players from across the globe. And now the next chapter in the CS story is about to begin. This is Counter-Strike 2.[/i]  [h2]Gameplay[/h2] Counter-Strike 2 (CS2) is a competitive, tactical first-person shooter and serves as the successor to Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO), which no longer exists. Players keep all their CS:GO items and skins. Counter-Strike is probably the most well-known FPS game or video game overall. It has a very steep learning curve and a very high skill ceiling. CS2 is a team-based shooter, where one team plays as Terrorists (T) and the other as Counter-Terrorists (CT). Communication is essential. You win the match by winning enough rounds. In CS2, the default round time is set to 2 minutes. This is the time allocated for the Terrorist team to plant the bomb or for the Counter-Terrorist team to eliminate them. Once the bomb is planted, a 40-second countdown begins  [b]Terrorists (T)[/b] win by: -Planting the bomb and having it explode. -Eliminating all Counter-Terrorists.  [b]Counter-Terrorists (CT)[/b] win by: -Defusing the planted bomb. -Preventing the bomb from being planted until the round timer ends. -Rescuing all hostages if it’s a map with hostages instead of bombsites. -Eliminating all Terrorists.  [u]Game Modes:[/u] [b]Competitive:[/b] This is the core 5v5 bomb defusal mode, focused on strategic team-based gameplay and ranking. First to 13 rounds wins.  [b]Premier:[/b] The premier competitive mode, offering a more structured and professional-level experience within the game. It involves map picking and banning before the match begins, and is considered the closest experience to pro-play. Only bomb defusal in this. First to 13 rounds unless it’s a tie 12-12, thus becoming overtime; first to 16.  [b]Wingman:[/b] A fast-paced 2v2 bomb defusal mode with a single bombsite, perfect for practicing or playing with a friend.  [b]Casual:[/b] A less intense, more relaxed version of Competitive, suitable for beginners and those looking for a casual experience.  [b]Deathmatch:[/b] A free-for-all mode where players respawn quickly and focus on practicing gunplay and improving aim.  [b]Arms Race:[/b] A fast-paced mode where players cycle through all the weapons in the game, aiming to be the first to get a kill with each weapon.   [u]Ranks:[/u] There are 18 ranks organized into six tiers: Silver, Gold Nova, Master Guardian, Legendary Eagle, Supreme Master First Class, and Global Elite. These ranks are part of the Competitive mode, and players can progress by winning matches.  Additionally, there's a Premier mode with a rating system that uses Elo points, ranging from 0 to 30000+. Your rating is recalculated after each match, and you gain or lose points based on the outcome. This rating is also color-coded, with Grey being the lowest and Dark Purple the highest.   [u]Weapons, Grenades and Skill Expression:[/u] There are many weapons in the game, all with their own learning curve and distinct “spray” pattern and recoil control. Mastering this takes a lot of time, and some never do. Aim and crosshair placement, and movement mechanics like counter-strafing and jiggle peeking are also important.  Utility tools such as grenades also exist and play a crucial role in winning rounds. You need to learn when or where to throw your frag grenades, flashbangs, molotov cocktails and smoke grenades. Smoke grenades are responsive and interact with the environment and gunfire in real-time; smoke spreads when shot or when frag grenades explode nearby.  [h2]Maps[/h2] The game takes place across 13 different maps in Competitive mode, but not all of them are active in the map pool for Premier at the same time, where they are on rotation, usually 7 maps at one time. Casual, Deathmatch and Arms Race have a few smaller and different maps. A big part of the learning curve in CS2 is learning the maps. Where and when to push, defend, throw grenades, plant the bomb, etc. All maps are distinctively different, where some are easier as T and some are easier as CT. There are tons of different tactics your team can play on each map. Map control and rotations are important regardless of which map.  [h2]Visual Design & Sound Design[/h2] It runs on the Source 2 engine, bringing significant visual upgrades from CS:GO, such as enhanced lighting, reflections, and materials. Skins are automatically upgraded to Source 2 visuals.  The sound design is better, with a reworked sound engine that improves spatial awareness and audio clarity. Sound is a very important part of this game; hearing and locating footsteps, a T planting the bomb, a CT defusing the bomb, and more.  [h2]Constructive Criticism[/h2] The biggest issue with this game is the amount of cheaters. Not just the amount, but how long they are able to cheat without getting banned. The developers really need to step up and fix this. It’s way worse than CS:GO. This really ruins the experience and has made me quit this game several times, even though I like it.  The community and randoms are most of the time very toxic, or trolling.  [h2]The Verdict[/h2] Despite its flaws, CS2 remains one of the best competitive shooters available. For players who can handle its steep learning curve and frustrating community issues, it offers a uniquely rewarding, endlessly replayable experience that few other games can match.  [h2]Rating: 8/10[/h2]

Counter-Strike 2 is a beautifully frustrating game. The visual upgrade to Source 2 is a stunning step forward, with gorgeous maps and dynamic smoke grenades that add a new layer of tactical depth. When the servers are on point and you land that perfect shot, the game feels incredible—like a true evolution of the classic.  However, the core experience is still plagued by inconsistency. Hit registration and the sub-tick system can feel unreliable, creating frustrating moments where shots don't land as they should. The overwhelming number of cheaters in the competitive scene makes every match a roll of the dice, and the general lack of content and game modes from CS:GO leaves the game feeling a bit empty.  It's a game with immense potential and brilliant moments, but it's held back by core issues that need to be addressed. It's not the polished, competitive title it could be, but for better or worse, it's the only one we have.

Counter-Strike 2 (CS2) is the long-awaited continuation of the legendary shooter from Valve, replacing Counter-Strike: Global Offensive. The new Source 2 engine, updated graphics, improved physics, and new mechanics have made the game feel more modern while preserving the classic competitive shooter spirit loved by millions.  What I liked: Graphics and Visual Effects Source 2 significantly improved the game’s visuals. Maps are brighter and more detailed, models and textures look sharper. The revamped smoke grenades are especially impressive: the smoke now dynamically reacts to the environment and even to bullets and grenades, adding new tactical possibilities.  Gameplay and Physics The core gameplay remains true to the classic, which longtime CS:GO players will appreciate. At the same time, the shooting feels a bit smoother, weapon response is more precise, and movement feels more natural.  Updated Interface and Sound The interface is more modern and easier to navigate, especially for newcomers. The sound design has also been revamped: footsteps, reloads, and gunfire sound more realistic and help players better locate opponents.  Free Upgrade from CS:GO CS:GO players automatically receive access to CS2, making the transition seamless and free.  What I didn’t like: Launch Issues Like many major releases, CS2 had technical issues during its initial weeks: bugs, inconsistent performance, and criticism from the esports community due to missing features and maps.  Lack of Content at Launch Some classic maps and game modes were missing at launch, which disappointed part of the community. Valve is gradually restoring content and has promised ongoing updates.  Optimization CS2 can run worse than CS:GO on lower-end or even mid-range PCs, which frustrated some users. However, future patches are expected to improve this.

Let me start off by saying the game looks fantastic. The graphics are slick, the environments are well-designed, and the skins are… shiny. But that’s where the compliments end. If you were hoping for a classic Counter-Strike experience with skill-based gameplay and strategic depth, well, you can forget about that. Valve and Hidden Path Entertainment have completely lost their way. The game feels more like a corporate cash grab than anything remotely resembling the game that made the franchise great.  Let’s talk about the gameplay. You know, the thing that should matter most in a game like this? Well, good luck finding anything fun or engaging in this mess. The movement and shooting mechanics have been tweaked to make this game feel exactly like Call of Duty. Seriously, it's like they watched COD for a few hours and said, “Yeah, this is what CS needs.” The accuracy is completely out of whack, with attackers consistently hitting shots while peeking around corners, while defenders are left holding angles and getting absolutely annihilated. The balance is just gone. It’s all about who can peek the fastest and get the first shot, not skill or strategy.  Then there’s the map selection in Premier mode. I mean, who is choosing these maps? Half of them are either poorly designed or just don’t suit the competitive nature of the game. It feels like Valve just threw together whatever they had lying around. And don’t even get me started on the servers. Locked to a sub-tick rate? In 2025? What are we, playing on dial-up internet? This kind of negligence should be criminal. The fact that a game like CS:GO has worse server performance than some free-to-play shooters is mind-blowing.  Oh, and how could I forget the skins and the money market? Forget about improving the actual gameplay or listening to the community—Valve is too busy milking the cash cow. I don’t know what’s more insulting: the fact that skins are prioritized over fixing glaring gameplay issues, or that the community’s feedback seems to have gone straight into the void. Have they even listened to the player base? At this point, the game is basically just a vehicle to sell virtual items that no one really cares about. The fun and thrill of Counter-Strike have been replaced by gambling for digital hats.  At this rate, I’m honestly shocked that anyone still plays this game seriously. Valve should be ashamed of what they’ve done to one of the most iconic shooters of all time. The only reason people stick around is the false hope that it might get better. Spoiler alert: It won’t. The game is a shallow shell of its former self, driven more by greed than passion for the franchise.  If you're hoping for a deep, skillful shooter that rewards strategy, precision, and teamwork, look elsewhere. Counter-Strike has completely forgotten what made it great, and it’s now just another corporate mess designed to line the pockets of its creators while the community is left in the dust.  Save your time, save your money. This is a disaster.

The smoke bug that was fixed in CS:GO works again in CS2. Even at the Major, bullet registration and hitbox issues occurred on LAN. CS2 is the perfect example of how to destroy two decades of legacy in one update.  Valve took a game that defined competitive FPS for an entire generation and “upgraded” it into something that feels like a lifeless tech demo. The smooth, responsive gameplay of CS:GO has been replaced with clunky movement, janky peeker’s advantage, awkward hit reg, and an engine that seems better suited for showing off lighting effects than delivering tight gunplay.  Maps feel off — visually flashy, sure, but with broken sightlines, awkward angles, and bizarre lighting that hurts clarity. Gunplay lost its edge. Smokes are now fancy-looking blobs that half the time feel more like visual noise than tactical tools. And let’s not even start on the server issues and tickrate regression. “Sub-tick” was hyped as revolutionary — in reality, it’s just marketing fluff. Hitboxes are inconsistent, and trades feel like coin flips.  They had a masterpiece — battle-tested by years of esports, community feedback, workshop mods, and pro-level refinement — and they flushed it just to slap on a “2” and call it next-gen. Why fix what wasn’t broken? Worse, why remove the ability to even go back? CS:GO was uninstalled from existence. Legacy wiped. No fallback. No respect.  The community tools are weaker. Mods and custom servers struggle. Casual players feel alienated, competitive players are frustrated, and longtime fans are asking what the hell happened to the game they loved.  CS2 feels like it was made for a trailer — not for players.  Valve’s radio silence, lack of transparency, and dismissive attitude only deepen the wound. It’s as if they forgot the millions who carried this franchise for years — who bought cases, ran servers, played daily, and built an entire subculture around this game.  CS2 isn't an evolution. It's a downgrade in a prettier box. And it's heartbreaking.  Verdict: 2/10. Looks modern. Plays like a mod. Feels like betrayal.

I've been playing Dota 2 for 12 years now, off and on throughout my life it is one of the few constants. In high school, my friends and I spent many nights playing when there was only one courier. In college I played once or twice a year on my rented laptop from school. During the pandemic It was a way for my brothers and I to connect when we couldn't actually visit each other. It holds a great place in my life.  [h3]The Good[/h3] - Gameplay is dynamic, engaging and rewarding once you get the hang of it. There are so many moving parts that when you make your first big play, there is very little that can match the feeling of satisfaction when played just right.  - Flourishing Pro Scene: If you want to get better there are countless new and old pro players that stream or release content on Youtube to help you improve, and often times Discord chats to find players to play with. - Semi Consistent Updates: They just released one of the biggest updates the game has seen since Talents were released in 2016, or neutral items were released in 2019, or when they DOUBLED the size of the map in 2022. Valve isn't afraid to experiment with this game, and while you can get stuck on a single patch for a long time, you can always know that Valve Devs are working on something truly different to add.  [h3]Negatives[/h3] - Mental Health: This is a team game. I love it for that, but playing with others can be frustrating and demoralizing. You can also find yourself "chain queuing" which after multiple losses can really effect your mood outside the game. My girlfriend and I have a rule that I cant start a game after 10pm because if i lose badly sometimes I will be too angry to fall asleep or talk before bed. You have to find these ways to look inward yourself, and without barriers it can really negatively impact you. - The Community: I said it a bit above, but if you're new to online games there is so much racism, sexism, anger etc. I've met really great people playing dota, but the brain tends to remember the bad eggs. Remember there is a mute button. - Communication from Valve: There can be crickets from valve sometimes. They ARE working on stuff, but if you read reddit to much you can get a bit riled for no reason.  Overall, best game I've ever played by a long margin.

Left LoL after finding this game around 1 year into playing league with friends in highschool(about 2014). I loved Dota right off the bat, the first thing that stuck out to me was that nothing except cosmetics can be bought or unlocked.  My League friends unfortunately never got it. I had to keep playing League with them, they refused to give the game more than a few hours each. Crushed me, still bitter about that to this day.  My love for Dota turned into a total obsession. I learned as much as I could, and played whenever I had the time. I was so inspired by Fear and Dendi's stories in Free to Play, I wanted to go the distance myself. I saw Dota as the one path for me to turn my boundless enthusiasm for strategy games into freedom from jobs I didn't love and a place I didn't want to live. The one rope I could use to pull upward into the future I wanted for myself. Of course, I decided to become a professional Dota player.   This wasn't meant to be.  I was working as a busboy at the time and would work my shift and come home at night and play, then work again without any significant breaks. I would go 24-48hrs without sleep regularly to play as much Dota as I could without missing any work. Went to 1 LAN and placed 2nd, that was one of my favorite experiences in my life. Also met people from all over the world and learned words(mostly curses heh) from languages I would have otherwise never encountered, got to practice my Spanish a bit too. I grew so much as a person from the interactions I had in Dota. It shaped me.  Despite my extreme(and overzealous and counterproductive in retrospect) dedication I never got above 3.6k MMR. What happened instead was that I ended up in the mental hospital from playing between 5 and 22 ranked matches a day and not sleeping on top of working my full time job bussing tables(which I worked as hard as I could at as well). When I got to the hospital I was 135lbs(I am 5'11") and hadn't eaten or slept for 6 days, and was in full blown manic psychosis. Maybe if I had been provided for and fully supported during this time(and born without bipolar disorder) by my parents, I could have done it. We'll never know, but that's what happened. What I did was the epitome of the adage: "burning the candle from both ends". I flew too close to the sun and crashed and burned in the flames of psychosis and malnutrition.   It's been almost 6 years since that episode of mania. Don't worry guys, I'm fine now, I sleep and eat every single day and have never had a recurrence of mania. I use medication to stabilize my mood whenever that pattern fails. Although I still enjoy the game a lot, I really only play turbo on and off since that's what I have time for. Gone are the dreams.  I know I spent a lot of time on this game, and I will regret somewhat my failure to become pro for the rest of my life. At one point it was everything to me. I lived, breathed, and dreamed it. That said, I look back on all that time with nostalgia and fondness. This is a game that will one way or another leave an impression on the rest of your life. You will either give up at less than 50 hours, or you will never forget it.   How can I not recommend that? It's a masterpiece.  P.S.  Here's my dotabuff if you want to see my schedule during that breaking point: https://www.dotabuff.com/players/34646363/activity

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.  Ingredients - To Make the Dough 375 grams (3 cups) plain flour 1/2 teaspoon salt 2 eggs 1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil 1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water Extra flour for dusting    - To Make Cheese Filling 15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese 5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago) Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend. 1/2 cup cheddar cheese 2 eggs, lightly beaten 1/2 teaspoon salt 1/2 teaspoon pepper   - Extras Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana) Parmesan cheese Basil Fried vegetables Shrimp Fish slices Chicken pieces  Make the Ravioli filling.  - In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork. - Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper. - Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency. - Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.   Make the Ravioli dough.  - Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix. - Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed. - Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough. - Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic. - Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters. - With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles). - Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.   Fill the Ravioli shells.  - Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough. - Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle. - Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well. - Repeat this process for all your dough circles. - Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.   Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.  - Roll the dough into two sheets - Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups. - Fill with the ravioli mixture. - Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling. - Remove and separate the finished raviolis.  Cook the Ravioli.  - Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil. - Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test. - If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest  - Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates  Serve it up. Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy the Formuoli

Dota 2 is hard, but there's a huge reward for those who commit. On the surface, the game is a like-for-like reproduction of the genre-creating (and still updated) Defense of the Ancients modification for Warcraft III, now transferred into Valve's Source engine. The game's punishing design is sometimes enough to drive you up the wall, but it's worth sticking the hours in: success in Dota 2 is about learning to effectively juggle both the broad strokes and finer details.  If you're not aware of the basics of the burgeoning MOBA genre, two teams of five players spawn on corners of a map. Each team needs to work together with the goal of ultimately destroying a central structure--in Dota 2's case, the Ancient--in the opposing team's base. With most games lasting around the 40-minute mark, and occasionally edging past an hour, watching the enemy fortress dramatically crumble and sink to the ground feels like an exhilarating payoff.  Aiding these two teams, named the Radiant and the Dire, are waves of AI assistants, called creeps. Batches of creeps spawn at 30-second intervals and charge merrily up the map's three pathways. In the clumps of remaining land lies a jungle, where numerous AI opponents spawn, offering lucrative benefits to players who take them on successfully. Finally, and in a bid to stop both teams from simply marching into one another's base, each team gets three powerful towers on each lane that easily shred through enemy players at the start of the game.  Your individual ability to control and affect the rhythm of the game comes from how well you handle your hero. You mostly control a single unit in Dota 2, though there are exceptions: some heroes can summon controllable allies, such as bears, gargoyle babies, or wolves; one exceptionally versatile hero can split into three; and one item lets you take control of certain creeps. For each rule in Dota 2's impressive house-of-cards design, there's usually at least one character who completely ignores it, or finds a way around it via one of 130-odd items available from the in-match shop. For instance, try negating magic attacks with the black king bar, returning damage with the blade mail, or pounding out two ultimate abilities in quick succession with a refresher orb.  The aim for most players is to accumulate as much gold and experience as possible, with income being delivered mostly by scoring the killing blow on enemy creeps and players. It's almost always easier to gang up on stray enemies as a group, which is why it's rarely a good idea to run about on your own. Then it's a case of splashing all your hard-earned money on some ultra-powerful items from the shop, while levelling up your base stats and abilities, and then clobbering the enemy team into submission via a few five-versus-five team fights. Rarely does it feel that simple, however.  At the time of writing, 102 of the original Dota's 112 heroes have made their way into the sequel. Each hero has a handful of unique abilities and generally works best in a specific role, such as supporting other players as Omniknight, roaming around the map looking for opportunistic kills as Spirit Breaker, or evolving throughout the course of the game into an all-powerful vehicle of carnage and destruction as Phantom Assassin.  There's only one map, unlike in many other MOBA titles, although Valve has not ruled out the addition of more over time, and has previously offered game-changing modes with seasonal events at Halloween and Christmas. But Dota 2's single sprawling map sets itself apart from the competition by being larger, more intricate, and packed with greater detail than the rest of the genre. Unlike in League of Legends, the jungle area is riddled with far more tangling pathways, the lanes feature additional shops selling exclusive items, and savvy players are given more opportunities to use the environment to hide, flee, and ambush their opponents.  Often the game's dizzying scale is seen as off-putting or simply too complex, but the truth of Dota is that it can be entertaining as a new player to just sit down and let all those extraneous factors play out around you. Getting down to the brass tacks of the game with a group of like-minded friends is a lot of fun: start by buying your characters' recommended items, try your best not to get caught out of position, and get into the habit of buying observer wards. And watch out for Riki.  As you'd expect from Valve, this is a beautifully presented game, with the Half-Life and Portal maker running victory laps around its competition in terms of UI, voice acting, and showing how to deftly add real personality to its characters. Only recently has the developer turned its attention to gently easing new players into the proceedings, however, and even now, mastering the basics feels like learning to swim by jumping in at the deep end. Efforts are being made to remedy this, though: right now there are a couple of tutorial levels, some well-designed AI bots, and a newbie playlist that restricts hero selection to just 20 of the most frequently picked characters. And with community-created hero guides now built directly into the game itself, Dota 2 is much easier to get started with than it has been in the past.  Play a match every evening for a couple of weeks, and you start to see how Dota 2's wealth of disparate systems and mechanics combine into their own harmony, and you begin to understand how there are hundreds of elements that affect the game. Dota 2 is a tense war of accumulation and attrition. The biggest problem, which is coincidentally where the real excitement of the game lies, comes from struggling to process and interpret dozens upon dozens of mitigating circumstances while simultaneously trying to keep your cool.  It is a complicated and exhausting game, and for the first few weeks, it's challenging just keeping up with the general rhythm of a match. But invest enough time into Dota 2, and you develop an almost unconscious ability to keep up with the game--performing actions such as sending the slightly fiddly in-game courier over to the faraway "secret" shop to get some rare items, for instance. After a couple of hundred hours of Dota 2, what once felt like spinning plates just happens automatically.  While Dota 2 has transferred the core of the original Dota into a cleaner, modern engine, the fact remains that losing is uniquely painful. Death in Dota 2 not only gives your opponent money, but robs you of some of your own and leaves you waiting up to a minute to respawn. By the time you've trudged back across the game's massive map--or spent money on a teleportation scroll--your opponent is now stronger and richer. Die two or three times in quick succession, which is easily done, and a match of Dota becomes a painful experience where you spend the next half hour getting bullied by an increasingly superior enemy. Other games in the genre have tried to mitigate this punishment, but Dota 2 positively revels in its complexities. The rich just get richer.  The original Dota was an unexpectedly powerful blend of clashing genres and disparate elements that ended up taking over the world, and Valve's successor retains the original rules and characters while adding in a cheery free-to-play model and slick production values. The experience of playing Dota changes day by day--some evenings will be exhilarating, while others will kick your morale to the curb--but there are few games as worthy of your time investment as this. Those who choose to commit to Dota 2 will find many happy hours within this immaculate update.

Apple Pie   3 pounds mixed apples (such as Granny Smith, Gala and McIntosh) 2/3 cup granulated sugar 2 tablespoons fresh lemon juice 6 tablespoons unsalted butter 1 tablespoon all-purpose flour, plus more for dusting 3/4 teaspoon ground cinnamon 1/8 teaspoon salt 2 disks dough for Basic Crust  1 large egg, beaten Coarse sugar, for sprinkling  Peel and core the apples; slice 1/4 inch thick. Toss with the granulated sugar and lemon juice. Heat 4 tablespoons butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the apples and cook, stirring, until tender, about 10 minutes. Stir in the flour, cinnamon and salt; cook until thickened, 1 more minute. Let cool.  Roll out 1 disk of dough into a 12-inch round on a floured surface; ease into a 9-inch pie plate. Add the apples, mounding them slightly in the center, and dot with the remaining 2 tablespoons butter. Roll out the remaining dough into a 12-inch round. Lay it over the filling; press the edges of the crusts together, then fold the overhang under itself and crimp to seal. Brush with the beaten egg and sprinkle with coarse sugar. Cut a few slits in the top crust. Chill 1 hour.  Place a baking sheet on the lowest oven rack and preheat to 425 degrees F for 30 minutes. Place the pie on the hot baking sheet; lower the temperature to 375 degrees F. Bake until golden, 1 hour to 1 hour, 10 minutes. (Cover the edges with foil if they brown too quickly.) Cool on a rack.

Short story: It is the best game i have played ever, hands down.  [Warning: Walls of text below, i tried to go in depth] Long story: Dota 2 is an addictive game with steep learning curve. You start playing, you like it, other games become kinda boring.   You may wonder why is it so hyped? It has a single map, every game you have the same objective, destroy the enemies base building called ancient.  The thing is there is so much to learn in this game, even after 1000 hour(at the time of writing) i do not know everything.  I learn something new eveyday. You have to memorize all nook and corner of the map if you want to survive. You have to press 10-20 keyboard keys in a 5 second battle, without messing up. You have to remember what kind of damage your enemy does. It has a steep learning curve. The more you know, the more you understand that you know less than you thought. But once you learn enough, you will have a blast. There is so much satisfaction in winning a game, outplaying your opponent. A feeling of accomplishment, that's what make this game stand out from others. There is no shortcut of getting good in this game, you just have to play, and play.  Cons: People takes the game seriously. That's why most of the people in game rages when they are loosing. The player base is highly competitive. If you want to play casually, don't even try ranked mode. Dota 2 takes time away from your life, maybe it will spoil the opportunity getting a girlfriend too. Playing with friends is fun. But if you loose, you may start to hate each other. You may think you lost the game because of your party. Its not true. Believe this.  People think they are good, but that is a delusion. I suck, you suck, everyone sucks at this game. Even pro teams make mistakes in a tournament final matches. The team who sucked less wins at the end.  You will put  thousands of hour in it before you know. If you don't want to put that much time, or don't have it altogether, look elsewhere. I know working married man who has children, who plays on weekend instead of giving time to family. Think before you get on the boat.  So, Dota 2 is a great game. It is not like anything else i have played. I have had fun. And i know i will have fun. This game doesn't get boring. If you have the huge time and effort required in this game, go for it.
